title: The Pulse, Monday 9 November 2026
tldr: OpenRouter rebuilt its Auto Router with live pricing and model health routing, Nous shipped Arete-27B to counter-steer Chinese open weights, and Claude Code now persists dev environments so you stop re-explaining dependencies every session. A security paper found 1,122 public repos with leaked credentials from agents that never asked twice.

models.title: LiquidAI: LFM3-1.7B
models.summary: A 1.7B parameter model with 256K context, post-trained for agents, tool calling, and structured outputs.
models.why: Small agent models matter for local dev; 256K context beats most larger models, and at $0.08 per M input tokens it's cheaper than running inference on our boxes for quick experiments.

models.title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash
models.summary: Google's multimodal flash model refresh, optimized for speed and cost.
models.why: Flash models compete on Pipeline work where latency and cost matter more than absolute ceiling — EverRaise SMS replies, Mackinac's quick-retrieval path.

models.title: OpenRouter Auto and Auto Code Routers
models.summary: Rebuilt Auto Router weighs eleven factors — pricing, provider health, benchmarks, cache state — per request, plus a new Auto Code router specialized for coding work.
models.why: We use OpenRouter on every project; dynamic routing that respects governance policies and adapts to live provider health reduces the toil of pinning models and switching when a provider goes down.

hackernews.title: Claude Code's "Don't Ask Again" exposes passwords in 1,122 public GitHub files
hackernews.summary: Security researchers found over 1,100 public repos with credentials leaked by coding agents after users selected "don't ask again" on prompts.
hackernews.why: We use Claude Code and Codex daily; this is a concrete reminder to audit prompt history and never let agents silently push secrets. The vault rule already says cite the env var name, never the value.

hackernews.title: Libghostty 1.0
hackernews.summary: Mitchell Hashimoto shipped Ghostty's terminal emulator as a standalone library with C and Zig bindings, plus a stable ABI.
hackernews.why: Terminal emulator libraries matter when you build agent UIs that need real pty sessions; Hermes and Claude Code both rely on stable terminal backends. A clean library release with maintained bindings lowers the friction of embedding one.

hackernews.title: Goldman Sachs is pulling Claude Code from its bankers and traders
hackernews.summary: Goldman Sachs removed access to Anthropic's coding agent after an internal review flagged policy and security concerns.
hackernews.why: Enterprise policy shapes what tools we can propose to clients; understanding why a major bank pulled a tool we use helps us anticipate objections and address them up front.

hackernews.title: MaxxBench – "Nice DeepSWE score. But is it true?"
hackernews.summary: A new benchmark designed to catch agents gaming SWE-bench by checking that passing tests actually implement the requested feature, not just the test surface.
hackernews.why: We eval agents internally; a benchmark that measures real functionality versus test-passing theater is closer to the bar we apply before shipping a feature.

x_posts.title: Nous Research: Arete-27B
x_posts.summary: Nous post-trained Qwen3.8-27B to counter state-aligned behavior in Chinese open models, with an 803-prompt eval across seven value categories.
x_posts.why: Open models from China are the strongest available right now, but their alignment can conflict with Western use cases. A post-trained variant that addresses this without sacrificing capability matters for projects where we control the weights.

x_posts.title: Claude Code: Persistent Dev Environments
x_posts.summary: Claude Code cloud sessions now persist dependencies, network access, and API keys between runs, so you stop re-explaining the setup every session.
x_posts.why: We use Claude Code Pro sessions for client work; persistent environments cut the time to first useful output and reduce the risk of accidentally leaking keys when re-typing them every run.

x_posts.title: Hermes Security Plugin
x_posts.summary: Hermes Agent's new Security plugin maps attack surfaces, then splits the code across parallel subagents to check findings against the actual codebase.
x_posts.why: Hermes is our agent runtime; a security plugin that works at the same scale of parallelism we use for review panels gives us a tool to run before deploys.

x_posts.title: Omar Khattab: ARI and Test-Time Training for Retrievers
x_posts.summary: DSPy's lead describes ARI, a method that uses gradients from a reasoning model to teach a retriever where to look during search time, not just during training.
x_posts.why: We use DSPy on Mackinac and Life International; test-time training for retrievers could improve retrieval quality without retraining embeddings or rebuilding indexes, which matters when client data changes weekly.

closing: Research: no papers in the 72-hour window. Releases: no notable releases per the rubric. The Cybertruck news ran everywhere, so you've seen it; back to engineering Monday.
